Senses.PreferredTarget: The one cannot be treated as present; the two cannot be treated as absent.
AlternateTargets: For one, do not assert being; for two, do not assert nonbeing.
SearchAliases: one not present two not absent Chan
one cannot have two cannot lack Zen
Senses.Note: Four current Tier 2 uses are preserved: Shiqi’s hall challenge, Tianru’s coffin-raising verse, Gulin’s response after a bow, and Liao’an’s New Year’s Eve address. Each master gives the pair a different immediate task; the sources do not equate one and two with a single fixed doctrinal pair.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，「一不得有，二不得無，一二之義，正在半途。有人道得恰好句麼？若道得，不惟雪竇有光，亦見汝衲僧家有明辨古今眼目；不然，總是隨例喫飯漢。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB183.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shiqi of Xuedou. Shiqi Tongyun opens a hall address with the numbered pair, then says that the meaning of one and two is still only halfway along. He challenges the assembly to supply a fitting sentence. If someone can do so, he says it will honor Xuedou and show a Chan practitioner’s eye able to distinguish ancient from present cases; otherwise they are merely eating by habit. Shiqi gives a test of discernment, not a final definition of what one and two stand for in every setting.

Occurrences.Kwic: 文監寺起龕文監寺起龕不立文字，不涉程途。政與麼時，如何是文監寺出門句子？一不得有，二不得無，倒跨楊岐三脚驢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1403.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianru Weize. At the raising of Monastery Director Wen’s coffin, Tianru Weize asks what line should accompany Wen as he leaves. Tianru then gives the pair and adds the image of riding Yangqi’s three-legged donkey backward. The first clause helps frame a departure that cannot be reduced to ordinary possession or absence; the backward donkey turns the funeral answer into a Chan image. The source records Tianru’s ritual wording, not a reply spoken by the deceased director.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧禮拜，師乃云：無心是道，道本無心；捨妄求真，真元是妄。以虗空為正體，法法全彰；將大地作禪床，頭頭合轍。所以道：法隨法行，法幢隨處建立。主丈橫分世界，草鞵踏斷乾坤。明明百草頭邊，突出衲僧巴鼻。一不得有，二不得無。摘楊花，摘楊花，三千里外無人會，種豆何曾得稻麻？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1412.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin Qingmao. After a monk bows, Gulin Qingmao says that mindlessness is the way and that seeking the true by casting out the false only makes another false distinction. He spans empty space and the earth, pictures a staff dividing the world and a monk’s face emerging among grasses, and says the numbered pair. He immediately follows it with a call to pick willow catkins and a reminder that planting beans will not yield rice or hemp. Gulin makes the compact formula part of a challenge about direct understanding and consequences; he does not give the audience a simple arithmetic or metaphysical equation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 除夜，進退兩序，小參。天寒歲晚，衲衣下事正好提撕；夜暗晝明，頂𩕳神光何妨顯露？以之建立化門，以之闡揚宗旨，以之布楊岐金圈，以之據南泉鉢位，以之回屋頭春色，以之植陰凉大樹，以之續照世燈，以之成佛子住，以之撥轉如來妙輪，以之揭示衲僧巴鼻。掀翻海岳，誰是知音？把斷要津，點頭自許。一不得有，二不得無，三十三天撲帝鐘，八臂那吒擎鐵柱。阿呵呵！釋迦老子與天帝釋相爭佛法甚閙，王老師忍俊不禁，打二十拄杖趂出。是則令不虗行，其奈將真珠作豌豆糶却本覺？雖是死馬醫，就中要妙。拈拄杖，卓一下，云：文殊、普賢，寒山、拾得，疥狗、泥猪，者白拈賊。喝一喝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1414.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liao’an Qingyu. On New Year’s Eve, while the incoming and outgoing monastic officers change places, Liao’an Qingyu gives a short address. He urges attention to the matter under the patched robe, lists ways it establishes and carries the teaching, then asks who can recognize its tune when mountains and seas are overturned. He speaks the numbered pair, follows it with a heaven-bell and Nezha image, jokes about Shakyamuni and Indra disputing the teaching, and strikes with his staff. The pair is one hinge in Liao’an’s present challenge to the assembly, not speech by those mythic figures or a routine statement about the officers’ jobs.

Senses.PreferredTarget: In the first and second nine-day winter spells, people meet without showing their hands
AlternateTargets: Through winter's first two nines, no one takes a hand out when meeting
SearchAliases: first nine second nine hands stay hidden
winter nines meet without showing hands
Senses.Note: The proverb names the first two nine-day cold periods of winter, when hands remain tucked away. Six masters use it in distinct present settings: birthday, mild-weather admonition, fundraising, hall appraisal, a cold-and-heat question, and a staff demonstration. Its seasonal meaning stays visible even when speakers turn “putting out a hand” into action or aid.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB454.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Pinjixiang. On his birthday, Pinjixiang Zhixiang answers the assembly’s congratulatory questions with jokes about his age, food and the place before his parents were born. In his own address he then gives the winter saying: during the first two nine-day cold spells, people who meet do not take their hands from their sleeves. He immediately asks what it would mean to put a hand out, turning the familiar seasonal line into a challenge about acting at the right moment. The proverb is Pinjixiang’s present answer, not a weather report or a reply supplied by the questioning monks.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. Tian’an Sheng quotes the winter saying at an evening gathering, but points out that it is the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, near the end of the first nine-day spell, and the weather is unusually mild. He says a winter without proper cold may bring illness next year, then shifts from bodily weather to the danger of a still-living furtive mind. Instead of striving to become a patriarch or buddha, he tells the listeners to return what is like soaked dead ash and settle their own home. The saying gives him a seasonally specific opening; his warning is directed at the assembly’s practice, not simply at uncovered hands.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB301.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Jiqi of Nanyue. Jiqi Hongchu quotes the cold-weather saying in a fundraising hall address. He jokes that people of old could keep their hands hidden because their storehouses had grain, whereas his own Huqiu community can scarcely secure the next meal. He spreads both hands and says that this old monk is putting his hands out; anyone wanting to gain merit should bring a gift promptly. The punch line depends on the literal hands in the proverb, while Jiqi uses it to ask for support. The request is his present action, not part of the inherited seasonal saying.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB362.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guantaoqi. After a monk asks Guantao Daqi four questions about taking or leaving person and scene, Guantao plants his staff and recites the winter saying. He follows it with a hidden golden hammer in a sleeve and with images of local farming and neighbors who live together like siblings. He says that long effort will eventually open the door, then asks why one would need further display or acrobatics. In this sermon the covered hand becomes a way to test when concealed force and simple local life are more apt than a showy answer; the line is Guantao’s address after the exchange, not the earlier monk’s question.

During a brush-holding dialogue, a monk asks Yikui Yuankui where cold and heat do not reach. Yikui answers with the winter saying. The monk presses him with the stock challenge that cold kills in cold weather and heat kills in hot weather; Yikui says this starts the matter all over again. When the monk calls it two, Yikui strikes and asks whether it is one or two, then tests the monk’s further claim of shared root. The proverb is Yikui’s first answer in this live exchange, so its cold-weather image is challenged rather than offered as protection from physical temperatures.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. At an evening gathering Yushan Shangsi recites the winter saying after promising to strip away his listeners’ borrowed postures. He taps his staff and imagines the cold making it leap into the hall, knocking over the unranked person and the original face. He ends by asking whether the drowsy assembly has awakened; no one answers, and he drives them apart with the staff. The hidden hands in the seasonal line are a starting image for Yushan’s forceful demonstration, while the leaps and collisions belong to his staged staff speech, not to an actual change in winter weather.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB454.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Pinjixiang. On his birthday, Pinjixiang Zhixiang answers the assembly’s congratulatory questions with jokes about his age, food and the place before his parents were born. In his own address he then gives the winter saying: during the first two nine-day cold spells, people who meet do not take their hands from their sleeves. He immediately asks what it would mean to put a hand out, turning the familiar seasonal line into a challenge about acting at the right moment. The proverb is Pinjixiang’s present answer, not a weather report or a reply supplied by the questioning monks.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. Tian’an Sheng quotes the winter saying at an evening gathering, but points out that it is the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, near the end of the first nine-day spell, and the weather is unusually mild. He says a winter without proper cold may bring illness next year, then shifts from bodily weather to the danger of a still-living furtive mind. Instead of striving to become a patriarch or buddha, he tells the listeners to return what is like soaked dead ash and settle their own home. The saying gives him a seasonally specific opening; his warning is directed at the assembly’s practice, not simply at uncovered hands.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB301.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Jiqi of Nanyue. Jiqi Hongchu quotes the cold-weather saying in a fundraising hall address. He jokes that people of old could keep their hands hidden because their storehouses had grain, whereas his own Huqiu community can scarcely secure the next meal. He spreads both hands and says that this old monk is putting his hands out; anyone wanting to gain merit should bring a gift promptly. The punch line depends on the literal hands in the proverb, while Jiqi uses it to ask for support. The request is his present action, not part of the inherited seasonal saying.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB362.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guantaoqi. After a monk asks Guantao Daqi four questions about taking or leaving person and scene, Guantao plants his staff and recites the winter saying. He follows it with a hidden golden hammer in a sleeve and with images of local farming and neighbors who live together like siblings. He says that long effort will eventually open the door, then asks why one would need further display or acrobatics. In this sermon the covered hand becomes a way to test when concealed force and simple local life are more apt than a showy answer; the line is Guantao’s address after the exchange, not the earlier monk’s question.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 兄弟九十日內打七打三，二六時中折旋俯仰，還知有恁麼事麼？若也知得，頭上安頭；若也未知，顢頇不少。要得覿體圓融，直須上無攀仰、下絕己躬，驀然卒地斷、爆地折，撒手那邊因行掉臂，自然開口道著、動步踏著，管取包天括地、籠古絡今，其如應時應節、契理契機，秉拂上座退身有分。何故聻？嶺上寒梅猶帶雪，溪邊嫩柳欲拖金。」復云：「昨日方丈和尚垂問，末後云：『以上七問，有人下語，轉轉相契，分付缽袋子；如轉轉不相契，亦付缽袋子。』眾中兄弟家商量道：『醍醐毒藥，一道而行。』又有道：『粟菽不辨，緇素不分。』又有道：『口甜心吝。』又有道：『慣設陷虎機關。』若然者，總未搔著老漢癢處在。殊不知，如將梵位直授凡庸，其奈捨父逃走者眾，遂致搭卻者話了也。揆上座今日將缽袋子一時搬向諸兄弟面前，力為保任去也。還有直下承當得底麼？」以拄杖拋下，云：「長安風月貫今昔，那箇男兒摸壁行？」秉拂。僧問：「朔風凜凜侵人面，寒雨霏霏透衲衣，公案現成且置不問，如何是寒暑不到處？」師云：「一九二九，相逢不出手。」進云：「秪如寒時寒殺闍黎，熱時熱殺闍黎，又作麼生？」師云：「又是從頭起。」進云：「與麼則有二也。」師打，云：「且道是一？是二？」進云：「天地與我同根，萬物與我一體。」師云：「作麼生是你同根體處？」進云：「六鑿未分誰擾擾？一爻纔動便紜紜。」師云：「不易念將來。」問：「拷鐘伐鼓，棒喝交加，無非是光影門庭施設邊事，枑如七佛已前，威音那畔更那畔，請師一句。」師云：「總被你道了也。」僧禮拜，云：「謝師答話。」師云：「切莫便承虛。」進云：「亙古亙今去也。」師便打，云：「下坡不走，快便難逢。」問：「箇箇金毛師子子，師今秉拂又何宣？」師云：「拄杖重重為你決。」進云：「秪如掀倒禪床，喝散大眾，又作麼生？」師云：「三十年弄馬騎，今日卻被驢子樸。」進云：「與麼則雪獅火裏翻身轉，石馬河頭飲水回。」師云：「不信道。」乃云：「山頭浪潑天，海底紅塵起，面壁老臊胡，何曾有直指？有直指，耳裏何曾容滴水？無直指，眼裏無筋貧。一世恁麼舉揚，還有共相委悉底麼？若也相委，連城不必重添五彩；若也未委，且聽葛藤曲直。」驀展拂子，云：「若論當人者著子，當陽無向背，歷劫絕盈虧，頂門頭輝天鑑地，腳跟下十字縱橫，日月未喻其明，冰雪難方其潔，天不能蓋、地不能載，何堪不自知休？
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB388.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yikui of Shending. During a brush-holding dialogue, a monk asks Yikui Yuankui where cold and heat do not reach. Yikui answers with the winter saying. The monk presses him with the stock challenge that cold kills in cold weather and heat kills in hot weather; Yikui says this starts the matter all over again. When the monk calls it two, Yikui strikes and asks whether it is one or two, then tests the monk’s further claim of shared root. The proverb is Yikui’s first answer in this live exchange, so its cold-weather image is challenged rather than offered as protection from physical temperatures.

In his own address he then gives the winter saying: during the first two nine-day cold spells, people who meet do not take their hands from their sleeves. He immediately asks what it would mean to put a hand out, turning the familiar seasonal line into a challenge about acting at the right moment. The proverb is Pinjixiang’s present answer, not a weather report or a reply supplied by the questioning monks. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Praise of the Orthodox Lineage of the Five Houses (五家正宗贊). The biography explicitly introduces this as Tianyi Yihuai's breakthrough verse; the verse opens with the ascending count before the line about standing alone before a ten-thousand-fathom peak. This is a transmitted quotation in a stronger container, not direct authorship of the container by Tianyi.

Senses.Explanation: One, two, three, four, five, six, seven is the ordinary ascending count. Tianyi Yihuai opens his breakthrough verse with the sequence before saying that he stands alone before a ten-thousand-fathom peak; the later Complete Five Lamps preserves the same use with the fuller account of his water-carrying pole breaking. Shiqi Tongyun opens a spring hall verse with the count and immediately identifies the day as the seventh day of the first lunar month (人日). In a New Year address, Muchen Daomin follows the count with the earthly branches from the fifth through the eleventh and says that counting straight through to the donkey year still does not get out. The records therefore use the unchanged schoolroom sequence in verse and calendrical speech without assigning it a separate symbolic definition.

Senses.Note: Five independent current Tier 2 uses retain the ascending and descending count. It serves a memorial challenge, retreat opening, fiftieth-birthday address, New Year’s Eve exchange, and another birthday question. Each speaker’s next question or action limits the meaning; the numbers have no single fixed secret referent across these passages.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB183.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shiqi of Xuedou. In a memorial hall address, Shiqi Tongyun raises the old case of Yantou ferrying people across a river and a woman who throws her child into the water after challenging him. Shiqi asks whether anyone can see where the woman stands; understanding that, he says, would illuminate the person being commemorated. He strikes his staff and counts one through seven and back, then speaks of the matter being clear even at a hair’s tip. The count is Shiqi’s present message to the mourners after his question, not words spoken by Yantou or the woman in the cited story.

Occurrences.Kwic: 「今朝是初八。」下座。付臥雲禪人上堂。「披衣登法座，識者合知歸。問著曹源路，君當為指揮。」遂授衣拂，下座。章婆子請上堂。舉：「臺山婆子，凡有僧問：『臺山路向甚麼處去？』婆云：『驀直去。』僧纔行，婆云：『好個師僧！又恁去。』趙州聞，云：『待我去勘破這老婆。』州如前問，婆如前答。州回，謂眾云：『這老婆被我勘破了也。』」師召眾云：「前後問答一般，且道那裡是他勘破處聻？」眾無語。師云：「未出門時先動棒，猶然遲卻幾多時。」僧問：「勘破婆子即且置，覿面提持事若何？」師云：「背後的一場懡㦬。」僧禮拜起云：「咦！夜深不向蘆灣泊，迥脫中間與兩頭。」師云：「氣急殺人。」下座。結制上堂。拈香云：「此一瓣香，冤有頭，債有主，偶爾狹路相逢，至今恨入骨髓，熱向爐中，供養象田堂上即念老和尚，用酬法乳之恩。」斂衣就座，僧問：「大開爐煹，鋾鑄聖凡，末後重關，請師拈出。」師云：「但得雪消後，自然春到來。」乃云：「盡道今日結制，山僧今朝結舌。結制與結舌是同？還是別？一二三四五六七，七六五四三二一，搕󵉿堆邊蘿蔔頭，十字街前攤瓦礫。擬心於此覓玄微，管保驢年猶未徹。」喝一喝，下座。晚參解制晚參。僧問：「一句了然，如何得脫塵離垢？」師云：「團團離海嶠，漸漸出雲衢。」進云：「恁麼則蓋天蓋地去也。」師便打云：「不出山僧這一棒。」乃舉：「洞山云：『諸兄弟！東去西去，直須向萬里無寸草去。』有者道：『出門便是草。』又有道：『不出門，亦是草芊芊地。』」師云：「二尊宿恁麼答話，未免落草；山僧不解落草，諸人不得草草。要識洞山麼？一句明明都說了，行人莫與路為仇。」晚參。僧問：「如何是大道？」師云：「恁麼大道？」僧無語，師便打，乃云：「大道只在目前，要且目前難睹。既在目前，因甚麼難睹？薰風自南來，殿角生微涼。」示眾因絕糧，師密至湖中打化歸，示眾。「鐵錘無孔向空拋，多少時流陷寂寥，大道若無過量者，如何留得到今朝？」法語掛鐘板法語掛鐘板法語。「昨日有今朝，今朝有昨日，昨日與今朝，切忌生分別。莫分別，板是木，鐘是鐵，輕輕擊著俱漏泄。」遂鳴。示密嚴定書記示密嚴定書記南禪師住黃龍四十年，坐鎮道場，不動聲色。今人住一破院，逞僥倖，爭人我，遂使攪壞叢林，分煙散眾，有傷法門規範，深望吾徒萬勿鹵莽。近時學人有多種病，捨迷求悟是病，避喧求靜是病，好名為人是病，好
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB192.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daxiu Zhu. At the opening of the retreat, Daxiu Zhu asks whether binding the retreat and having one’s tongue bound are the same thing. He counts from one to seven and back, places a radish beside a dung heap and broken tiles at a crossroads, and warns that anyone searching there for hidden profundity will still not have penetrated it even in the year of the donkey. The reversed count is one of Daxiu’s deliberately plain answers to his own opening question; he does not supply a secret numerical code to decode.

When a patron requests a hall address for Xinyue’s fiftieth birthday, Baichi Xingyuan counts up to seven and back and says the days remain clearly good whether numbered forward or backward. He then removes seven and picks up one, saying that even eight-armed Nezha and thousand-eyed Great Compassion could not grasp it. After rejecting elaborate descriptions, he points instead to eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, sitting at ease and sleeping when tired, and finally taps his staff. The count sets up this birthday challenge about what can be found in ordinary life; the divine figures are examples in Baichi’s speech, not speakers of the headword.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB419.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Bu’yanle (Huayan). On New Year’s Eve a monk comes out, and Buyan Daole says “Not that, not that” and strikes when the monk hesitates. Holding his staff across, Buyan counts up to seven and back, says the forward and reverse sequence would continue into days without end, and asks for a word for seeing out the old year and welcoming the new. He answers with the old year’s lamp being blown down and the new calendar opened. The numerical reversal joins a real change of year to a challenge about the turning point; it is Buyan’s present verse after the exchange, not the silent monk’s reply.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB475.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Jingtingsong. In a short address requested for Juexia’s birthday, Jingting Dezong counts one through seven and back and says that from beginning to end the counting could continue through many lifetimes. Although the numbers are clear, he asks who can truly distinguish what is at their center. Here the backward count is part of Jingting’s birthday question about recognition amid repeated time. It is his own utterance, distinct from the person whose birthday brought the gathering together.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB183.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shiqi of Xuedou. In a memorial hall address, Shiqi Tongyun raises the old case of Yantou ferrying people across a river and a woman who throws her child into the water after challenging him. Shiqi asks whether anyone can see where the woman stands; understanding that, he says, would illuminate the person being commemorated. He strikes his staff and counts one through seven and back, then speaks of the matter being clear even at a hair’s tip. The count is Shiqi’s present message to the mourners after his question, not words spoken by Yantou or the woman in the cited story.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. When a patron requests a hall address for Xinyue’s fiftieth birthday, Baichi Xingyuan counts up to seven and back and says the days remain clearly good whether numbered forward or backward. He then removes seven and picks up one, saying that even eight-armed Nezha and thousand-eyed Great Compassion could not grasp it. After rejecting elaborate descriptions, he points instead to eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, sitting at ease and sleeping when tired, and finally taps his staff. The count sets up this birthday challenge about what can be found in ordinary life; the divine figures are examples in Baichi’s speech, not speakers of the headword.

On New Year’s Eve a monk comes out, and Buyan Daole says “Not that, not that” and strikes when the monk hesitates. Holding his staff across, Buyan counts up to seven and back, says the forward and reverse sequence would continue into days without end, and asks for a word for seeing out the old year and welcoming the new. He answers with the old year’s lamp being blown down and the new calendar opened. The numerical reversal joins a real change of year to a challenge about the turning point; it is Buyan’s present verse after the exchange, not the silent monk’s reply.

Senses.Explanation: One person transmits a falsehood and ten thousand transmit it as fact describes repetition turning an unfounded report into accepted fact. The saying appears as Bie'an Xingtong's own answer and as Xinghua Cunjiang's inherited reply about what should be discussed before Duozita. Shiyu Mingfang closes an address with the maxim; Yushan Shangsi answers a visitor with it; Wuyi Yuanlai supplies it in his self-answered sequence. Baichi separately raises Xinghua's Duozita reply.

Senses.PreferredTarget: One person passes on a false report; ten thousand pass it on as fact
AlternateTargets: One person spreads a fiction, and ten thousand repeat it as truth
SearchAliases: one false report ten thousand repeat as fact
Senses.Note: Six current uses warn that repeated accounts can acquire unearned authority. The immediate targets differ: Shiyu’s imagined objection, Danxia’s burning-Buddha anecdote, Wuyi’s temple question, Shanhui’s later transmission claims, Baiyu’s ancestral-hall proof, and Tianshu’s secondhand awakening story. Each master uses the proverb to test a particular claim.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB190.xml). Dharma Platform of Chan Master Shiyu. Shiyu Mingfang asks the assembly what makes the many ordinary tasks of monastery life a skillful current, then imagines someone objecting that such an account sweeps away Bodhidharma’s lineage. He asks whether to accept that objection: accepting it betrays one’s own insight, while rejecting it erases earlier sages. He ends with the proverb that a false report started by one person becomes accepted by ten thousand, followed by a shout. The saying is Shiyu’s warning about a ready-made judgment in this hall discussion, not an actual claim he is asking the audience to repeat.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. A monk asks Baichi Xingyuan why the monastery director in the famous story of Danxia burning a wooden Buddha lost his eyebrows. Baichi says the event never happened and tells him not to malign the ancients. When the monk replies that the case is recorded, Baichi answers with the proverb about one false report being repeated as fact. He challenges the authority of an inherited anecdote in this exchange; the proverb belongs to Baichi’s reply, not to Danxia or to the questioning monk.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB197.xml). Essentials of the Recorded Sayings of Master Wu Yi of Boshan. Wuyi Yuanlai poses four questions and gives his own answers. For the third, he asks why a corner of the Buddha hall is missing and replies that one person spreads a false report and ten thousand treat it as fact. Unlike a historical explanation of damaged architecture, this is Wuyi’s deliberately unsettling answer to his own question. The neighboring three questions receive similarly oblique replies, so the proverb warns the listener against turning an easy account of what is seen into certain knowledge.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB223.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shanhui. In written guidance for the secretary Shizhi Tong, Shanhui Huan says Bodhidharma came east to point people toward rest and direct seeing of their own nature. He then says later people passed on unfounded accounts until a multitude treated them as fact, describing elaborate claims about transmission without words and the proliferation of branches as things people say came from Bodhidharma. Shanhui urges his addressee to settle the matter before the story of an arrival and to work as an unencumbered practitioner. The proverb criticizes Shanhui’s later tradition bearers, not Bodhidharma’s own speech.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB359.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baiyu. At the ancestral hall during the opening of a new monastery, Baiyu Jingsi says that one person passes on a false report and ten thousand pass it on as fact. He calls the resulting accounts in China and India a great muddle, asks what would verify them, and answers by offering incense with a mantra. The line is Baiyu’s present challenge at an ancestral shrine: it asks what proof underlies inherited claims while his ritual gesture supplies the local response. It is not attributed to the patriarchs pictured in the hall.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB399.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianshuzhi of Helin. In a Buddha-birthday hall address, Tianshu Xingzhi starts with the proverb, then says everyone repeats that Shakyamuni awakened on seeing the morning star twenty-five centuries ago. He observes that such a story arouses joy, aspiration and reverence, then turns to the assembled listeners: those who take it up are themselves appearing to teach in many forms. He ends by asking them not to wrong Shakyamuni through a merely distant story. The proverb opens a challenge to secondhand belief; Tianshu does not simply deny the birthday account as a historical fact.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB190.xml). Dharma Platform of Chan Master Shiyu. Shiyu Mingfang asks the assembly what makes the many ordinary tasks of monastery life a skillful current, then imagines someone objecting that such an account sweeps away Bodhidharma’s lineage. He asks whether to accept that objection: accepting it betrays one’s own insight, while rejecting it erases earlier sages. He ends with the proverb that a false report started by one person becomes accepted by ten thousand, followed by a shout. The saying is Shiyu’s warning about a ready-made judgment in this hall discussion, not an actual claim he is asking the audience to repeat.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. A monk asks Baichi Xingyuan why the monastery director in the famous story of Danxia burning a wooden Buddha lost his eyebrows. Baichi says the event never happened and tells him not to malign the ancients. When the monk replies that the case is recorded, Baichi answers with the proverb about one false report being repeated as fact. He challenges the authority of an inherited anecdote in this exchange; the proverb belongs to Baichi’s reply, not to Danxia or to the questioning monk.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB197.xml). Essentials of the Recorded Sayings of Master Wu Yi of Boshan. Wuyi Yuanlai poses four questions and gives his own answers. For the third, he asks why a corner of the Buddha hall is missing and replies that one person spreads a false report and ten thousand treat it as fact. Unlike a historical explanation of damaged architecture, this is Wuyi’s deliberately unsettling answer to his own question. ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 居士懋德曰：「山僧住持六剎，接待海眾，常內外清振，上下和平，由有矩侍者故也。正如鸞鳳之有羽翼，湖海之有舟楫，雖九霄之曠，四溟之淵，未有不至其極。凡學道輔叢林，正宜如此。不然，何以使荊棘叢林轉為道德叢林？」山僧近見他剎法綱不振、聲譽不揚，每自太息，甚至涕出。盍末法時代，人多澆浮，而主叢林者，賢不肖不擇，可謂哲人乎？於是癸未閒，以衣缽囑矩傳化，今十二年矣。余暇日未常不切慕臥龍之言。爾既職是任，將來所得無涯，但不可因循。後日，學不如矩，誰之過邪？真如以圜木為枕，策勵己躬，然後道尊德貴，千古師範。古人巨欺我哉！余得爾弼，雖所職頗當，然要以道業為先。不先以道業，不能垂範湖海，後世取法。余又聞之，天地以道生育萬物，聖人以德感化民心，故道德古今定衡，學道人不可不拳拳者。古今得之以王，失之以亡，非今日也。明教有言：「尊莫尊乎道，美莫美乎德。」此之謂也。示石芝仝書記示石芝仝書記達磨東來，不為別事，只要與人指箇休歇田地，謂之直指人心，見性成佛。後來一人傳虛，萬人傳實，卻道不傳而傳、不說而說，即是西來大意。卻又分宗列派，種種施設，都道從彼得來。殊不知阿魏無真、水銀無假，有甚著落處？不如向他未來時一切坐斷，不獨成佛有餘，亦謂之無事道人。我書記石芝，魏安人也，以風塵不偶，脫卻鶻臭布縿，來與者夥人仝學西來大意。忽一日，山僧上堂結座畢，書記云：「還家不上長安路，一任風華雪月揚。」山僧便下座。因來求法語，山僧意以為將來或有用處，因記他兩語於此，庶書記他日不孤山僧一種苦心，山僧亦不孤書記參學苦也。吁！分明不是家常事，卻道家常更是誰？示端居泰書記示端居泰書記「東廁屋裏漫攃珍珠，瑪腦盆中無著驢糞」，此山僧昔畣書記語也。如今要得正法流通，須看從橫作用，則門風始不致委地也。臨濟眼如走電，德山口似血盆，無此人有此法，終不能垂範萬世。端居泰公自蜀中二千里來見聖恩，以從橫機辦挑聖恩無礙三昧，臨濟、德山腳手將來亦或及之。一日，入室乞法語，聖恩不欲孤之，乃書此言以進之，異日紹隆吾宗，一條棒惡辣有日在。噫！閣外滄江晚，林邊月色初。示大雲長維那示大雲長維那靈山四十九年拖泥帶水，吐盡縣河機辦；少林幾萬里來赤縣神州，費盡許多鹽酢。後之人謂之說法利生，殊不知靈龜曳尾而跡愈多。昔人有言：本自無瘡，勿傷之也。大雲長公維那入社火求道

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB399.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianshuzhi of Helin. In a Buddha-birthday hall address, Tianshu Xingzhi starts with the proverb, then says everyone repeats that Shakyamuni awakened on seeing the morning star twenty-five centuries ago. He observes that such a story arouses joy, aspiration and reverence, then turns to the assembled listeners: those who take it up are themselves appearing to teach in many forms. He ends by asking them not to wrong Shakyamuni through a merely distant story. The proverb opens a challenge to secondhand belief; Tianshu does not simply deny the birthday account as a historical fact.

Senses.Explanation: A claim passed on by one person can be repeated by ten thousand as though it were fact. Shiyu Mingfang asks the assembly what makes the many ordinary tasks of monastery life a skillful current, then imagines someone objecting that such an account sweeps away Bodhidharma’s lineage. He asks whether to accept that objection: accepting it betrays one’s own insight, while rejecting it erases earlier sages. He ends with the proverb that a false report started by one person becomes accepted by ten thousand, followed by a shout. The saying is Shiyu’s warning about a ready-made judgment in this hall discussion, not an actual claim he is asking the audience to repeat. A monk asks Baichi Xingyuan why the monastery director in the famous story of Danxia burning a wooden Buddha lost his eyebrows. Baichi says the event never happened and tells him not to malign the ancients. When the monk replies that the case is recorded, Baichi answers with the proverb about one false report being repeated as fact. He challenges the authority of an inherited anecdote in this exchange; the proverb belongs to Baichi’s reply, not to Danxia or to the questioning monk. Wuyi Yuanlai poses four questions and gives his own answers. For the third, he asks why a corner of the Buddha hall is missing and replies that one person spreads a false report and ten thousand treat it as fact. Unlike a historical explanation of damaged architecture, this is Wuyi’s deliberately unsettling answer to his own question. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB223.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shanhui. Shanhui Huan owns the retained deployment, ruling the blessing is not only the one man's blessing and the realm at peace but gives every patched-robe under heaven eyes to see and ears to hear — tongue cut sooner than touch the sovereign's taboo.

Senses.Explanation: The one man's blessing of the Chan records: the throne's festive stamp — set on the New Year and the installation incense, granted by season-knowing monks, jabbed with, and ruled to open every patched-robe's eyes. Zhenjing Kewen, after the donor's gifting of a canon edition, hears the monk grant the one man's blessing with the myriad leaning on it and rules the monk knows the season well, Fushi Tongxian at the year's opening answers the blessing-line question with the one man's blessing, the myriad people leaning on it — gold branches forever thick through three thousand worlds, jade leaves ever spread through ten thousand ages — Minshu Ruxiang welds the formula to the buddha-choosing field: one man's blessing, myriad people staying, the choosing-field open, the emptied mind passing the list — and Konggu Daocheng at his Chongqing installation hangs the blessing on the succession: imperial sons and grandsons passing it on forever, the one man's blessing, loyal civil and military ministers honored generation after generation. Mingjue Cong in the palace hall hears the auspicious air rise — the hall of ten-thousand goods, the one man's blessing equal to heaven and earth — and answers that even so one must know the debt, Chaozong Tongren remembers the verse he once dared present his late teacher — the Hanlin academician soaked through, the war minister cold to the bone, no need to keep crying grievance face to face: the one man's blessing, the myriad people at ease — and the teacher's answering verse he then judged lacking in reserve, Muchen Daomin at the Tiantong installation wishes the one man's blessing and the realm at peace, every guest at the feast touching the unborn's purport, and Shanhui Huan rules the New Year blessing is not only the one man's blessing and the realm at peace but gives every patched-robe under heaven eyes to see and ears to hear — tongue cut sooner than touch the sovereign's taboo.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一人發真歸元，十方虛空悉皆消殞

Senses.PreferredTarget: When one person returns to the source, the void in all ten directions vanishes
SearchAliases: when one person returns to the source, the void in all ten directions vanishes
Senses.Note: This Śūraṅgama line is invoked in five distinct recorded contexts. Yinyuan includes it in a monk’s abilities, Yunwai asks why space remains, Guantao asks why Mount Tiantai still stands, Huiyue contrasts later revisions, and Shanyi asks where the visible world would go. The line’s scriptural attribution and each later speaker’s question are distinct layers.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB193.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan. At the release of the retreat, Yinyuan Longqi describes a true monk’s force through inherited feats: drinking the West River in one gulp, a shout that deafens for three days, and this line about one person returning to the true source so that space in the ten directions disappears. He adds the overturned foot of Shuilao and then addresses the assembly as people able to bind and release, kill and give life. Yinyuan uses the scriptural line in a forceful catalogue before asking who will follow; he is not reporting that the physical sky has vanished during the gathering.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB280.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yunwaize of Shending. In a short address Yunwai Xingze explicitly raises two lines from the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, including the headword, whose original voice the record presents as the Buddha’s. Yunwai asks why the three realms and visible space remain if the many teachers of past and present have truly returned to the source. Nobody answers. He strikes his staff and offers the images of moving flowers with butterflies and buying a stone with clouds attached. The scriptural line is the premise of Yunwai’s pointed question, not a claim that his audience has observed the disappearance of the world.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB362.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guantaoqi. Guantao Daqi makes the scriptural line the opening of a verse-question: if one person’s return to the source dissolves space in every direction, why does Mount Tiantai still stand so visibly? His poem answers with a mountain rising toward the moon and sky, visitors on a level field, and a road whose unevenness appears when the mountain is pushed over. Guantao is composing a challenge from the inherited wording; the mountain’s continued visibility is the difficulty he puts before the listener, not a contradiction he silently ignores.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB418.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huiyue Xu. Huiyue Xu explicitly cites the Śūraṅgama Sūtra’s headword and then places three Chan revisions next to it. Wuzu Fayan says space is struck and bumped; Yuanwu Keqin says it gains flowers upon brocade; Huiyue says space is torn open and kneaded together. He follows with another scriptural saying and questions whether even the Buddha’s wording gives a Chan practitioner a place to stand. The exact retained headword is the scripture’s attributed line, not Huiyue’s different replacement; Huiyue’s current action is to test it by comparison.

In a hall address Shanyi Ruchun recites the headword and immediately asks where mountains, rivers, trees and the whole array of sentient and nonsentient things could be put if space vanished. He offers deliberately difficult alternatives for placing them, waits, strikes the teaching seat and ends with willow strands that cannot be gathered into one hand. Shanyi uses the inherited line as a live question about what remains visible, not as a prediction that the landscape will literally disappear for the assembly.

Senses.Explanation: When one person realizes the true source, the scripture says, space in all ten directions disappears. At the release of the retreat, Yinyuan Longqi describes a true monk’s force through inherited feats: drinking the West River in one gulp, a shout that deafens for three days, and this line about one person returning to the true source so that space in the ten directions disappears. He adds the overturned foot of Shuilao and then addresses the assembly as people able to bind and release, kill and give life. Yinyuan uses the scriptural line in a forceful catalogue before asking who will follow; he is not reporting that the physical sky has vanished during the gathering. In a short address Yunwai Xingze explicitly raises two lines from the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, including the headword, whose original voice the record presents as the Buddha’s. Yunwai asks why the three realms and visible space remain if the many teachers of past and present have truly returned to the source. Nobody answers. He strikes his staff and offers the images of moving flowers with butterflies and buying a stone with clouds attached. The scriptural line is the premise of Yunwai’s pointed question, not a claim that his audience has observed the disappearance of the world. Guantao Daqi makes the scriptural line the opening of a verse-question: if one person’s return to the source dissolves space in every direction, why does Mount Tiantai still stand so visibly? His poem answers with a mountain rising toward the moon and sky, visitors on a level field, and a road whose unevenness appears when the mountain is pushed over. Guantao is composing a challenge from the inherited wording; the mountain’s continued visibility is the difficulty he puts before the listener, not a contradiction he silently ignores. Huiyue Xu explicitly cites the Śūraṅgama Sūtra’s headword and then places three Chan revisions next to it. Wuzu Fayan says space is struck and bumped; Yuanwu Keqin says it gains flowers upon brocade; Huiyue says space is torn open and kneaded together. He follows with another scriptural saying and questions whether even the Buddha’s wording gives a Chan practitioner a place to stand. The exact retained headword is the scripture’s attributed line, not Huiyue’s different replacement; Huiyue’s current action is to test it by comparison. Senses.Note: Four current Tier 2 settings use this wording of the inherited line: Tianyin’s person-and-scene answer, Fushi’s standing-temple challenge, Yinyuan’s comparison with a Confucian saying, and Linquan’s commentary on a time before an empty aeon. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin. A monk asks Tianyin Yuanxiu four questions about taking away person and scene. For the third, where both are taken away, Tianyin answers with the line that one person’s return to the true source makes all worlds in the ten directions disappear. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB185.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fushi. Fushi Tongxian quotes the saying and asks whether Sanxian Temple still exists if the worlds in every direction have disappeared. When the assembly gives no answer, he raises another old case about whether something survives the fire at the end of an age and asks whether that reply actually helps anyone. The assembly’s answers still do not satisfy him; after further questioning, he says the help is like throwing a solid iron hammer with no hole straight at someone. The temple question is Fushi’s present test of a literal reading, not a report that the building has vanished.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB193.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan. In a hall address Yinyuan Longqi speaks about maintaining the right eye through hardship and finding one clear point that illuminates every place. He pairs the inherited line about one person returning to the source and the ten-direction worlds disappearing with Confucius’ saying that restraining oneself and returning to ritual makes the world return to humaneness. Yinyuan uses both to argue for complete, immediate clarity, then challenges conventional descriptions of Shakyamuni’s awakening. The headword is part of this comparison, not a claim that the physical world disappeared before his listeners.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1303.xml). Elder Linquan’s Commentary and Chanted Remarks on Master Touzi Qing’s Verses on Ancient Cases: Empty Valley Collection. Linquan Conglun comments on an old case about the time before an empty aeon. He voices the line about one person returning to the source and the ten-direction worlds disappearing and asks why one would have to wait for a remote pre-cosmic time. He then urges an opening where verbal formulas and discrimination have run out, before a sound is made, and says it is hard to find anyone who can receive such a tune. The line is Linquan’s present reply to the old case’s temporal framing, not speech by the earlier case figures.

Occurrences.Kwic: 嘆奇哉，秖為明星現，瞎驢長禍胎。大眾還知麼？昨夜釋迦老子覷破天上一點明星，天上明星照破釋迦老子面孔，今日供佛飯僧，楊居士已在睹明星時同成佛了也，現前大眾盡大地人總在睹明星時同成佛了也。當年釋迦老子恁麼見得透，走出雪山，即以這一點明星照定世間人面目，觀法先後次第，建立無邊行門，談經三百餘會、說法四十九年，成一代時教，正眼看來，大似一翳在眼，空花亂墜。山僧恁麼批判，還有為釋迦老子出氣者麼？如有，卻與他同一鼻孔；如無，徒讓廣嗣舌頭。咄！且道諸人眼睛在什麼處？」以拄杖指云：「明星一點今猶在，照破面門待幾時？」拍膝，下座。省我馬居士請上堂。僧問：「當門按劍，魔佛齊揮；頂𩕳具眼，群機洞照。抹過上頭關人來，和尚作麼生管帶？」

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. Yushan Shangsi owns the retained deployment: the whole teaching of one lifetime — on inspection, a worn straw sandal.

Senses.Explanation: The whole teaching of one lifetime — forty-nine years and three hundred sixty assemblies gathered into one pile, then weighed by the Chan answers that would rather say it to one, quote the primer's first line, or call the whole thing a worn straw sandal. The case core. A monk asks Muzhou Daoming: what is the whole teaching of one lifetime? He answers: top-great-man, Q-Yi-Ji — the first characters a child learns to write, set against the whole canon. Yuanwu Keqin, commenting on the twin case in the Blue Cliff Record: a monk asks Yunmen the same; Yunmen says — say it to one. The school's stream, wanting to know the point of the buddha-nature, must watch the season and conditions; this is called the transmission outside the teaching, the mind-seal singly handed down, pointing straight at the mind for seeing the nature. Old Sakyamuni, forty-nine years in the world, three hundred sixty assemblies, opening the talk on sudden and gradual, provisional and real — call it the whole teaching of one lifetime. This monk lifts it up to ask: what is it? Why did Yunmen not explain it all for him, instead telling him — say it to one? And Wuzu Fayan, raising the same case in the hall: the monk asks Yunmen; Yunmen says — say it to one. Says the master: say it to one — it rolls up the whole five thousand forty-eight; wind, flowers, snow, and moon let themselves be handed down; behind the vajra head, raw iron is added. Zhongfeng Mingben, in the mountain-hut night talks, marks the pile as the learner's trap: the second kind of relapse — or else one takes the whole teaching of one lifetime as proclaimed by the Buddha's own mouth — since my work on the bearing phrase is not quick, I cannot but trace the lines and count the ink, planting good seeds as I go, telling myself none of it is wasted — all of it, he rules, is deserting right faith and wandering to the far shore of the odd arts. And Hanyue Fazang, lying pillowed on stone in the pines, hands the preaching to the ten thousand sights: clouds blaze, water and stone clash, the Vairocana body shows, the broad long tongue comes out — days called di-lan, days called a-bu-shi, days when the fourth-month sudden clearing makes the mountain colors good, one first dawn and the bird-sounds multiply — none of this is within the jurisdiction of the whole teaching of one lifetime; today the ten directions speak as mouth — mountain-say, water-say, empty-say, being-say, the living and lifeless of three times all turning the wheel together, so that hearers and seers stand on the spot and become buddhas. Lianyue Daozheng, at the twelfth-month eighth-day assembly: year after year the eighth of the last month, the praise is spoken — wonder of wonders — only because the morning star appeared, and the blind donkey is ever the womb of trouble. Old Sakyamuni saw through the one point of morning star in the sky; the morning star in the sky shone through old Sakyamuni's face; today's offering to the buddha and feeding of the assembly — the layman Yang already became buddha together at the moment of seeing the star, and the whole great earth's people before me too. Back then he saw it so thoroughly, walked out of the snow mountains, and with that one point of morning star fixed the world's faces: after the way was seen, the gates of conduct were built without edge — three hundred-odd assemblies of sutra-talk, forty-nine years of preaching, completing the whole teaching of one lifetime; but to the correct eye it looks most like an eye-film in the eye, flowers falling in empty sky. Does anyone breathe on Sakyamuni's behalf? If so, he shares one nostril with him; if not, the wide-heir tongue is left idly wagging — Pa! And Yushan Shangsi, after the catechism of true buddha, true way: the whole teaching of one lifetime — on inspection, what is it but a worn straw sandal? A great-spirited man never leans on it for his understanding: sometimes the shout that scatters white-cloud vapors, sometimes the tongs that break open the hammer of empty sky — not only the three worthies blanched and the ten stages startled: even if old Sakyamuni himself came, he too would be chased off to some other world; only then does one count as a man no delusion can hold.

Senses.Explanation: One stroke of a blade leaves two separate pieces: the image is a single completed cut rather than repeated or partial cutting. Ying'an Tanhua and Longtan Zhiyuan make that compact result a short public answer; Dahui Zonggao makes it a direct command; Fenyang Shanzhao calls for a 'one-cut-two-pieces person'; and Changqing Huileng checks the formula by saying that even one cut into two pieces does not yet qualify someone as a lineage teacher. These named answer, command, person-label, and critical uses establish a reusable formula and the Chan bend while leaving the figurative object unspecified.

Senses.Explanation: The all-times locator: no special hour — what is asked of the learner is asked in every moment alike. Linji Yixuan tells the hall that whoever comes is not shortchanged — yet do not go sorting it out wrongly in any moment, for understanding or not understanding, it is all wrong, and let the whole world strip it off him; Huangbo Xiyun in the Wanling record says: in every moment, in walking, standing, sitting, lying, aim only at no-mind, with no sorting, no leaning, no lodging, drifting dumb-faced all day like a man no one knows; Huineng tells the verse-writer that supreme awakening must see its own mind at the word's fall, thought after thought in every moment, ten thousand things unblocked, one true and all true; the bloodline treatise of Bodhidharma answers the no-mind questioner: every act and every move, in every moment and every place, is your own original heart, your own original buddha. Guishan Lingyou's assembly instruction, kept in Dahui's treasury, sets the practitioner's heart plain and unfeigned — sight and hearing ordinary in every moment, eyes not shut, ears not stopped; Yunmen Wenyan on the road asks an old host how to make things out in every moment, gets the question thrown back — call what an every-moment? — and answers that Sakyamuni has already said it and Maitreya still does not know; Baichi Xingyuan turns Linji's old address over with Yuansou Xingduan's comment and rules his own: in every moment sort it out as it comes, not a hair wrong; Tianran Hanshi tells his assembly not to be carried around by false thoughts and dreamt-up notions in any moment, answering affairs without setting anything up.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin: In a letter to the layman Cao Nianzi, Tianyin Yuanxiu responds to repeated reports of suffering. He says that rich and poor alike are caught in trouble, then quotes the Buddha's complete Diamond Sutra verse about conditioned things as dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning. Tianyin applies the quotation to body and mind, rank, wealth, and affliction: seeing their lack of fixed reality lets one act amid ordinary demands without being mastered by them. The verse is the Buddha's inherited speech; the explanation and advice to Cao are Tianyin's own.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Poshan: In Poshan Haiming's hall sermon, a monk first asks about the true character of things and receives a blow. Poshan then tells the assembly that he had dreamed of lay visitors Yin and Dai asking him to preach. He calls family, property, official rank, awakening, and even release dreams before quoting the complete Buddha verse. Poshan immediately asks what an open-eyed dream is, leaving the assembly without an answer. When Yin later kneels and asks him to explain, Poshan strikes him and withdraws. The citation starts the live test; the blow is Poshan's response, not part of the Buddha's verse.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Expanded Record of Chan Master Cishou Huaishen: In Cishou Huaishen's hall sermon, the Buddha's complete verse is recited first: conditioned things are to be seen as dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows. Cishou then turns the instruction into his own question: if that is how conditioned things are viewed, how should the unconditioned be viewed? His answer invokes an obstruction in the eye that even a skilled physician cannot pick out. The pair in the headword belongs to the earlier quoted verse; Cishou is the later questioner and commentator, and the eye image is his local challenge to treating the scriptural formula as a finished answer.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fangrongxi: In a short instruction, Fangrong Ruxi asks what the 'king of the teaching who breaks existence' actually reveals. He tries several familiar doctrinal verses as possible answers, including the complete Diamond Sutra verse with these dream, illusion, bubble, and shadow images. Each is framed as 'Could it be this?' Fangrong says that merely answering in that way would let talkative teachers borrow the title without showing their own understanding. He closes by saying the wooden elder, his staff, will have to test anyone claiming more. The verse is inherited Buddha speech raised as a candidate, while the series of questions and the proposed test are Fangrong's.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Qiran Zhi: In a hall sermon requested by the layman Lü Yinghui and other visitors, Qiran Chaozhi says that delight in scenery can become attachment as soon as choosing and rejecting arise. He explicitly introduces the complete verse as spoken by the World-Honored One at the assembly on complete discernment. Qiran then tells the gathered laypeople that their differing practices, including precept keeping and Chan inquiry, still fall within the circle he is discussing. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin: In a letter to the layman Cao Nianzi, Tianyin Yuanxiu responds to repeated reports of suffering. He says that rich and poor alike are caught in trouble, then quotes the Buddha's complete Diamond Sutra verse about conditioned things as dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning. Tianyin applies the quotation to body and mind, rank, wealth, and affliction: seeing their lack of fixed reality lets one act amid ordinary demands without being mastered by them. The verse is the Buddha's inherited speech; the explanation and advice to Cao are Tianyin's own.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Poshan: In Poshan Haiming's hall sermon, a monk first asks about the true character of things and receives a blow. Poshan then tells the assembly that he had dreamed of lay visitors Yin and Dai asking him to preach. He calls family, property, official rank, awakening, and even release dreams before quoting the complete Buddha verse. Poshan immediately asks what an open-eyed dream is, leaving the assembly without an answer. When Yin later kneels and asks him to explain, Poshan strikes him and withdraws. The citation starts the live test; the blow is Poshan's response, not part of the Buddha's verse.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Expanded Record of Chan Master Cishou Huaishen: In Cishou Huaishen's hall sermon, the Buddha's complete verse is recited first: conditioned things are to be seen as dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows. Cishou then turns the instruction into his own question: if that is how conditioned things are viewed, how should the unconditioned be viewed? His answer invokes an obstruction in the eye that even a skilled physician cannot pick out. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fangrongxi: In a short instruction, Fangrong Ruxi asks what the 'king of the teaching who breaks existence' actually reveals. He tries several familiar doctrinal verses as possible answers, including the complete Diamond Sutra verse with these dream, illusion, bubble, and shadow images. Each is framed as 'Could it be this?' Fangrong says that merely answering in that way would let talkative teachers borrow the title without showing their own understanding. He closes by saying the wooden elder, his staff, will have to test anyone claiming more. The verse is inherited Buddha speech raised as a candidate, while the series of questions and the proposed test are Fangrong's.

Senses.Explanation: The Buddha's Diamond Sutra verse compares conditioned things to a dream, illusion, bubble, and shadow, then adds dew and lightning. Six later Chan records quote the same line in different settings: Tianyin counsels a suffering layman, Poshan turns it into a live test, Cishou asks about the unconditioned, Fangrong questions borrowed formulas, Huijue applies it at a memorial, and Qiran addresses lay visitors. In each witness, the verse's original speaker differs from the named master who raises and applies it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J23/J23nB134.xml). Recorded Sayings of the Five Houses (Selections). Yunmen Wenyan is invited to a meal by the official Chen Shangshu, who asks what a traveling monk’s work is beyond Confucian books and scriptural specialists. Yunmen turns the question back: what is the teaching’s intent beyond colored scrolls and words that fall silent? When Chen cannot answer, Yunmen asks whether he reads the Lotus Sūtra, quotes its line that all livelihoods and productive work do not conflict with reality, and asks how many inhabitants of the neither-perception-nor-nonperception heaven lose their place. Chen again falls silent and bows after Yunmen warns him against a hasty claim to understanding. The headword is an explicitly marked scriptural quotation inside Yunmen’s test, not Chen’s answer or a standalone endorsement of every job.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin. Tianyin Yuanxiu retells Yunmen’s same exchange with Chen Shangshu and inserts his own comments between its turns. Where Chen is pressed about the teaching beyond scrolls, Tianyin proposes a sharper answer he would give in Chen’s place. After Yunmen quotes the Lotus livelihood line and asks about the highest formless heaven, Tianyin again supplies a hypothetical reply, then says Yunmen wielded a keen sword and Chen had to submit to its testing. The exact headword remains the Lotus wording quoted by Yunmen in the old case; Tianyin’s present action is to appraise and recast the official’s missed responses, not to author a new scriptural saying.

Occurrences.Kwic: 言須會宗，勿自立規矩。舉：雲門到江州，陳操尚書請齋，纔見便問：「儒書中即不問，三乘十二分教自有座主，作麼生是衲僧行腳事？」門曰：「曾問幾人來？」曰：「即今問上座。」門曰：「即今且置，作麼生是教意？」曰：「黃卷赤軸。」門曰：「這箇是文字語言，作麼生是教意？」曰：「口欲談而辭喪，心欲緣而慮忘。」門曰：「口欲談而辭喪，為對有言；心欲緣而慮忘，為對妄想。作麼生是教意？」書無語。門曰：「見說尚書看《法華經》，是否？」曰：「是。」門曰：「經中道：『一切治生產業，皆與實相不相違背。』且道非非想天有幾人退位？」書無語。門曰：「尚書且莫艸艸，三經五論，師僧拋卻，特入叢林，十年二十年尚不奈何，尚書又爭得會？」書禮拜曰：「某甲罪過。」無著頌作家慣戰不齎糧，奪鼓攙旗勢莫當。虎驟龍驤誰辦的，反思仁義勝剛強。玅湛頌調將埋兵幾戰征，尚書空使口頭爭。三千劍客今何在，嬴得悲風動地生。靈瑞頌袖裏金鎚劈面來，左旋右轉趁風雷。韶陽因謗斯經故，直得披毛戴角回。舉：法眼聞齋魚，問僧：「還聞麼？適來若聞，如今不聞；如今若聞，適來不聞。」無著頌

Occurrences.Kwic: 中會取，直透萬重關，不住青霄中。先了却那邊，却須這邊行履。何故？不因今日事，爭話昨夜夢？恁麼參到徹取，而自由自在。衲僧若未然，爭奈喫鐵棒何？還吾平生粥飯來。故經曰：若不見佛知見，未出凡夫境；若悟入佛知見，不出三界出。貪嗔痴一句，了然道著，分明許你作大活計。畢竟還恁麼也，公私分曉。長安道：示眾曰：大乘妙法蓮華經，字字含玄感應新。舉起一卷玉軸，則瞿曇鼻孔人人皆収手裡；拈取一經太意，則諸佛正眼箇箇悉在心中。絲毫許無移易，毛髮許無滲漏。故經曰：一切治生產業，皆與實相不相違背。若恁麼，大地有情悉是同時成道作佛去。且道誰人如此？頭長三尺，頸短二寸。示眾曰：教意親參，祖意正到。祖意親參，教意正到。祖教不二，意句無別。雖然與麼，實到此田地始得。若未到，切忌舉教拈祖，知趣能有幾人？故經曰：此眾無枝葉，唯有諸貞實。增上慢人，退亦佳矣。若然，向上一路，千聖不傳，是向上人而應辨得。初心未改，還同後心，則又何愁不會？人人須是發悟。諸佛中未了漢名眾生，眾生中了義漢名諸佛。所以達磨大師曰：直指人心，見性成佛。如何是正？當恁麼時
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1428.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Jingci Huihui. In a separate recorded sermon, Zide Huihui praises the Lotus Sūtra as a teaching whose words point toward the Buddha’s own seeing. He explicitly cites its line that all livelihoods and productive work do not conflict with reality, then says that, taken through, all sentient beings would awaken together. He asks who could meet that claim and answers with a deliberately odd bodily image before moving to the relation between scriptural and ancestral intent. The retained words belong to the scripture as quoted by Zide; his current sermon tests how to realize them rather than treating the mere fact of working as sufficient.

Senses.Explanation: The Lotus Sūtra says that ordinary livelihoods and productive work need not stand apart from reality. Yunmen Wenyan is invited to a meal by the official Chen Shangshu, who asks what a traveling monk’s work is beyond Confucian books and scriptural specialists. Yunmen turns the question back: what is the teaching’s intent beyond colored scrolls and words that fall silent? When Chen cannot answer, Yunmen asks whether he reads the Lotus Sūtra, quotes its line that all livelihoods and productive work do not conflict with reality, and asks how many inhabitants of the neither-perception-nor-nonperception heaven lose their place. Chen again falls silent and bows after Yunmen warns him against a hasty claim to understanding. The headword is an explicitly marked scriptural quotation inside Yunmen’s test, not Chen’s answer or a standalone endorsement of every job. Tianyin Yuanxiu retells Yunmen’s same exchange with Chen Shangshu and inserts his own comments between its turns. Where Chen is pressed about the teaching beyond scrolls, Tianyin proposes a sharper answer he would give in Chen’s place. After Yunmen quotes the Lotus livelihood line and asks about the highest formless heaven, Tianyin again supplies a hypothetical reply, then says Yunmen wielded a keen sword and Chen had to submit to its testing. The exact headword remains the Lotus wording quoted by Yunmen in the old case; Tianyin’s present action is to appraise and recast the official’s missed responses, not to author a new scriptural saying. A case collection repeats the Yunmen–Chen Shangshu encounter in full, including Yunmen’s explicit Lotus quotation and Chen’s failure to answer the follow-up question about beings in the highest formless heaven. Three different verse authors then respond: Wuzhuo praises a seasoned fighter, Miaozhan faults the official’s verbal contest, and Lingrui imagines a hammer brought straight to the face. Those poems show later reactions to the case but do not make the verse writers the speakers of the retained Lotus line. This is a parallel transport of the same old exchange, not an independent new encounter. Occurrences.Kwic: 各由見解深淺。不以調與不調之行而定法義。偏圓但自隨病對治。不須讚此毀彼二密意破相顯性教說前教中所變之境既皆虛妄。能變之識豈獨真實。心境互依空而似有故也。且心不孤起。託境方生。境不自生。由心故現。心空即境謝。境滅即心空。未有無境之心。曾無無心之境。如夢見物似能見所見之殊。其實同一虛妄都無所有。諸識諸境亦復如是。以皆假託眾緣無自性故。未曾有一法不從因緣生。是故一切法無不是空者。凡所有相皆是虛妄。是故空中無色。無眼耳鼻舌身意。無十八界。無十二因緣。無四諦。無智。亦無得。無業。無報。無修。無證。生死涅槃平等如幻。但以不住一切無執無著而為道行。諸部般若千餘卷經。及中百門等。三論廣百論等。皆說此也此教與禪門泯絕無寄宗全同。既同世尊所說菩薩所弘。云何漸門禪主及講習之徒。每聞此說。即謗云。撥無因果。佛自云。無業無報。豈邪見乎。若云佛說此言自有深意者。豈禪門此說無深意耶。若云我曾推徵覺無深意者。自是汝遇不解之流。但可嫌人。豈可斥法。此上一教據佛本意雖不相違。

Senses.Explanation: All phenomena is an unrestricted plural expression governed by its surrounding predicate. A quoted Laṅkāvatāra verse says that all phenomena are unborn; Guifeng Zongmi states that all phenomena are empty because none arise apart from causes and conditions; and Mazu Daoyi says that a single mind gathers all phenomena.

Senses.Explanation: The formula says that all dharmas are unborn or do not arise. Yongming Yanshou directly sets the formula inside an argument about arising and non-arising: “if all dharmas do not arise, the perfection of wisdom arises.” He immediately warns that treating non-arising as a fixed interpretation becomes another bondage.

AlternateTargets: No phenomenon truly comes into being, and none truly passes away
SearchAliases: all phenomena neither arise nor cease Chan
no arising no ceasing all things Buddha teaching
Senses.Note: The pair states that all phenomena neither arise nor cease. Foyuan challenges a merely inherited repetition; Huiyue and Tianran apply it to changing appearances. Shanduo, Jifei, and Qibai make it the opening of separate present teachings before adding images or questions. The second clause is needed: nonarising alone can sound like absence, while the paired source turns continue to show events and responses.

In an evening talk Foyuan Chegang announces that all phenomena neither arise nor cease, then rebukes old Gautama for calling gold iron and jokes that Bodhidharma had nowhere to hide but went east. He offers the same tiny coin whether anyone can strike down these two old masters or cannot, then ends with frost and snow images. The pair is Foyuan's present, deliberately provocative opening; the later Yunmen case in the same KWIC is a separate example, not its speaker.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB406.xml). At a bathing-the-Buddha sermon, Tianran Hanshi says all phenomena neither arise nor cease, yet appear as conditions gather, like flowers in a mirror or the moon in water. He raises his staff and asks the assembly whether they see the Buddha passing before their own faces, then strikes the staff and asks whether they hear. His visible and audible demonstrations make the pair a question about how appearances are met, not a claim that nothing can be seen or heard.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB414.xml). In a teaching after returning to Donglin, Shanduo Zhenzai voices the pair, then points to the mountain outside, rain striking pear blossoms, and butterflies flying. A monk immediately asks what Buddha is and what lies beyond Buddha; Shanduo answers first with a scorched seed that cannot sprout, then with changing clouds and a downpour. The opening pair belongs to Shanduo's present teaching, and the following questions test it against ordinary sights and the monk's categories.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB425.xml). In a reply addressed to the Chan student Xihe, Jifei Ruyi opens with the pair. He says there is no single phenomenon to discard or grasp and that both Buddha and sentient beings are provisional names; if Xihe's eyes open, he will laugh quietly. In an evening talk Foyuan Chegang announces that all phenomena neither arise nor cease, then rebukes old Gautama for calling gold iron and jokes that Bodhidharma had nowhere to hide but went east. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB406.xml). At a bathing-the-Buddha sermon, Tianran Hanshi says all phenomena neither arise nor cease, yet appear as conditions gather, like flowers in a mirror or the moon in water. He raises his staff and asks the assembly whether they see the Buddha passing before their own faces, then strikes the staff and asks whether they hear. Senses.Explanation: All phenomena neither arise nor cease: six teachers voice this paired line while meeting appearances, questions, and their own listeners. In an evening talk Foyuan Chegang announces that all phenomena neither arise nor cease, then rebukes old Gautama for calling gold iron and jokes that Bodhidharma had nowhere to hide but went east. He offers the same tiny coin whether anyone can strike down these two old masters or cannot, then ends with frost and snow images. The pair is Foyuan's present, deliberately provocative opening; the later Yunmen case in the same KWIC is a separate example, not its speaker. On his first evening at Ganlu, Huiyue Xu says many streams enter one sea and diverse things enter one true teaching. He voices the paired line, extends it with neither existence nor nonexistence, and immediately names mountains, light and dark, sentient and insentient things as endlessly speaking. He asks the brothers whether they hear this and answers that the Buddha seals the direct root while he cannot seek it by plucking leaves and twigs. Here the pair holds equality and the visible variety together in his current address. At a bathing-the-Buddha sermon, Tianran Hanshi says all phenomena neither arise nor cease, yet appear as conditions gather, like flowers in a mirror or the moon in water. He raises his staff and asks the assembly whether they see the Buddha passing before their own faces, then strikes the staff and asks whether they hear. His visible and audible demonstrations make the pair a question about how appearances are met, not a claim that nothing can be seen or heard. In a teaching after returning to Donglin, Shanduo Zhenzai voices the pair, then points to the mountain outside, rain striking pear blossoms, and butterflies flying. A monk immediately asks what Buddha is and what lies beyond Buddha; Shanduo answers first with a scorched seed that cannot sprout, then with changing clouds and a downpour. The opening pair belongs to Shanduo's present teaching, and the following questions test it against ordinary sights and the monk's categories. In a reply addressed to the Chan student Xihe, Jifei Ruyi opens with the pair. He says there is no single phenomenon to discard or grasp and that both Buddha and sentient beings are provisional names; if Xihe's eyes open, he will laugh quietly. The line is advice to this named student about clinging to categories, rather than an anonymous sermon or a report that visible things disappear. He adds that at this point even the mouth of the senior monk might as well be hung on the wall, making verbal explanation inadequate beside what the phenomena show. The next hall sermon, beginning with a shout, is a separate address; its question to the assembly does not belong to this headword occurrence.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB466.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baishan Kai of Shanxi. Senses.Explanation: The line from the morning star: how strange — all beings are endowed with the thus-come one's wisdom and virtue-marks, only by deluded thinking and clinging do they fail to attain it. The whisk at Baishan's hall hears it and laughs out loud — quite right, very apt — yet dares guarantee the old brother is not through. The telling and the plain price: Dahui Zonggao tells it whole — before the mountain of right awakening the morning star appeared and Shakyamuni suddenly woke; at the place he had verified he saw the great earth and all beings of one body with him, equal, and said the line: what I verified, the ten directions' buddhas and even the wriggling creatures attained all at once — and he set the ocean-seal at each person's heel; Huanyou Zhengchuan reads it round and empty — I observe all beings are endowed with the thus-come one's wisdom and virtue-marks but by deluded thinking and clinging do not verify it; with no clinging, is that not empty? — the Diamond's beings-beings are no beings beside it; Muyun Tongmen preaches the plain price — what is deluded thinking? just forgetting this one great matter; touch any place blankly and all one does and makes is deluded thinking; Zhu'an Zhenyan has his staff report it in a loud voice — the yellow-faced old man deep on the snow ridge lifted his head at midnight, suddenly saw the morning star, made much ado and said the line — and before the sound had ended: one film over the eye, sky-flowers falling in profusion — a slap of the staff. The halls that doubt it: Binya Jian grants the whole mechanism wholly bared, the root cut through — yet inspected closely, very much like stamping from a mold; Zishui writes to a layman — the old man of the snow mountain's one piece of bitter heart is to make people wake on the spot, but people simply will not: they neglect the ordinary and hurry to seek the lofty and deep, how lamentable; Baishan Dekai lifts the whisk — the yellow-faced one on the whisk-tip enters right settledness, sees the morning star, wakes, says the line — and the whisk cannot help laughing, crying quite right, very apt, yet I dare guarantee the old brother is not through.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一切眾生具有如來智慧德相，但以妄想執著而不證得

Senses.PreferredTarget: All beings have the Tathagata’s wisdom and qualities, yet deluded thoughts and clinging keep them from realizing it
SearchAliases: all beings have the tathagata’s wisdom and qualities, yet deluded thoughts and clinging keep them from realizing it
Senses.Note: The Buddha’s awakening statement says that all beings have the Tathagata’s wisdom and qualities but do not realize them because of deluded thought and clinging. Muyun uses it to urge his listeners to turn from worldly status toward the matter already present. Baichi explains the two halves in counsel to a laywoman, contrasting a constant light with habits of following sights and sounds. Baiyu quotes the statement on the Buddha’s awakening day, then asks whether the Buddha’s own movements could be called clinging too. Yuan’an goes further, questioning a fixed division between wisdom to gain and delusion to discard. The later sermons keep the original statement alive by testing what it means to possess yet not realize.

Occurrences.Kwic: 胡深旨。羅山云：「我這裏秪有一口劍，劍下有分身之意，亦有出身之路。」快哉斯言，知音者少，隨氀𣯜趁，大隊漢烏足以語此哉。示超奇善友示超奇善友人非生知，貴在力學，學而計之時日、積之歲月，未有不成者。設或一暴十寒，吾知其不能進矣。參禪亦然，時而鞭策，日而揣摩，歲月無虛度之功，終身有實證之驗。祖翁田地，四至契書，一一分明、一一了當，名為絕學，無為閒道人也。雖然無為無事人，猶是金鎖難，且道：節角在什麼處？試下一轉語看。示超慧陳氏夫人示超慧陳氏夫人一切眾生具有如來智慧德相，但以妄想執著而不證得，此是黃面瞿曇初證初得時大開口縫，為今古人立箇定案也。何名智慧德相？即當人一點常光，照天照地，最微最妙，至虛至靈，不可思議境界是也。何名妄想執著？即當人日用之中隨聲逐色，恣縱虛妄，胡思亂想，不可遏滅境界是也。妄想無暫停、執著無暫解，智慧德相如何得現前透露乎？所以善知識見人問著，不論是男、是女，便與劈頭拈出，宿有靈根底直下知歸，更不在絮絮忉忉。其或未能領略「父母未生前，如何是我本來面目」，且將這箇話端向行住坐臥處密密提撕，刻刻窮究，無絲毫

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB359.xml). On the Buddha's enlightenment day, Baiyu Jingsi recounts Shakyamuni seeing the morning star and quotes his exclamation that all beings have the Tathagata's wisdom but fail to realize it because of deluded thought and attachment. Baiyu immediately shouts and challenges the statement: he asks whether the Buddha's departure from home, awakening and many teachings would themselves count as deluded activity. He then favors eating when hungry and dressing when cold. The headword remains the Buddha's reported utterance; Baiyu uses it as the target of his provocative current sermon, not as his own unqualified doctrine.

Senses.Explanation: All sentient beings have Buddha-nature is a universal proposition that Zen records repeatedly place in the mouth of a questioner confronting Zhaozhou’s “no” about a dog. Its recurring job is not to close the issue by an inherited teaching but to sharpen a public contradiction: if the universal statement stands, why does Zhaozhou deny the dog? Later masters raise, redirect, or refuse that collision rather than supplying one uniform reconciliation.

Senses.Explanation: “Every sound is buddha-sound; every color is buddha-color” is repeatedly stated and then tested against concrete objects, noises, and seasonal sights. Yunmen Wenyan raises an unnamed source’s formula and tests it with a whisk; Sanyi Yu, Jiuzhao Lang, and Xiangya Ting extend it into heard and seen scenes. Yunmen Wenyan raises the unnamed formula, asks what the whisk is, and rejects simply calling it a whisk. Sanyi Yu follows the pair with bells, geese, leaves, and a lamp. Jiuzhao Lang places it after walls and rubble emit great light; Xiangya Ting follows it with willow eyes, peach lips, water bubbles, and reflected spring light.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J35/J35nB343.xml). Miyin Zhenchuan contrasts Gaofeng's long investigation and sudden break through doubt with imitators who attach themselves to a first glimpse and display clever Chan talk. To explain why such fixed seeing still blocks them, he quotes Yunmen's first illness, darkness everywhere with an object before one's face, followed by Yunmen's second illness of a subtle thing left after seeing emptiness. Miyin then cites Baiyun's warning that awakening still requires meeting a person who can test it. Yunmen supplies the quoted diagnosis; Miyin uses it to warn against treating an initial insight as finished understanding.

Pinjixiang Zhixiang raises Yunmen Wenyan's teaching on two illnesses of light and two of the dharma body, including the first illness of darkness everywhere and an object before one's face. He then tells serious students not to swallow the teaching whole: they should examine, in their own case, what the light is and why it fails to pass through. He explicitly calls the first condition delusion and asks them to examine the subtler second condition too. Yunmen is the speaker of the quoted headword; Pinjixiang makes it a present instruction in careful self-examination.

The headword is the first of Yunmen's light illnesses: no clarity anywhere, with an object set before one's face. Wenmu follows the whole quotation with his own four-line verse, then moves to a different old case. The illness formulation belongs to Yunmen's cited teaching; Wenmu's verse is a later response, not a second utterance of the headword. Pinjixiang Zhixiang raises Yunmen Wenyan's teaching on two illnesses of light and two of the dharma body, including the first illness of darkness everywhere and an object before one's face. He then tells serious students not to swallow the teaching whole: they should examine, in their own case, what the light is and why it fails to pass through. He explicitly calls the first condition delusion and asks them to examine the subtler second condition too. Yunmen is the speaker of the quoted headword; Pinjixiang makes it a present instruction in careful self-examination.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Everywhere bright and radiant
Senses.Note: The older tree case opposes flourishing brightness to withered plainness. Jiqi refuses to make either description decisive, and Yunsou revoices both sides while saying arising and ceasing have no separate mark to grasp. Xuefeng raises his staff and opens a way for the bright side. Muan joins brightness with freedom in every place; Chushi places it on the busy street against the stillness of a solitary peak. The phrase works because its apparent opposite remains in view.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB192.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daxiu Zhu. Daxiu Zhu owns the retained deployment, ruling the porridge and rice, the walking and sitting, each stirring and stillness all not in the bowl of the world, with Bodhidharma as fellow traveler for the one who knows.

Senses.Explanation: A paired unit naming each stirring and each stillness of the day, listed beside its sibling pairs and ruled on wherever the records locate the working. Ying'an Tanhua rules that to say the thus-come one is seen in the twelve double-hours' each stirring and stillness, word and silence, turn and bow is taking the thief for a son — and to say he is not discerned there is madness running outward; Mi'an Xianjie strings the pairs on the hall seat — one advance one retreat, one stirring one stillness, trust the naga ever in composure — with one seize one release, one kill one quicken, the Jiazhou elephant salt-heavy and the Shanfu iron bull thirsty; Wuzhun Shifan, before the assembly, holds that once the shapes of stirring and stillness cannot be found, each stirring and stillness, exit and entry, release and gather, advance and retreat is nowhere other than the playground of the uncanny light and freedom; and Cishou Huaishen, taking leave of the assembly, likens it to the wild crane's wheeling and the floating clouds' gathering and scattering — no north or south, no coming or going, the wayfarer's heart just so. Tianru Weize runs his own day before the assembly — rising, washing, porridge, sweeping leaves, watching the fish, one word one silence, one stirring one stillness — hawking the assembly's life-lord without pause through the six watches of day and night; Qianyan Yuanzhang ties it to the one sentence: today's doing clear, then each stirring and stillness, word and silence, rise and fall, birth and death — living just so, dying just so; Guting Shanjian hatches his bird on it — brooding without losing the clutch through stirring and stillness until the shell falls apart and the lively one hops out knowing hunger and fullness, feathers whole, flying where it will; and Daxiu Zhu, reversing Gaofeng Yuanmiao's bowl of the world, rules the porridge and rice, the dung and water, the walking and sitting, each stirring and stillness all not in it — know that and Bodhidharma becomes one's fellow traveler; miss it and one boils tea with water and cooks rice with rice.

Senses.PreferredTarget: A teacher of fifteen hundred people, yet he does not even grasp the point of the exchange
AlternateTargets: With fifteen hundred students, he still misses what this question is about
SearchAliases: Sansheng fifteen hundred teacher misses point exchange
Xuefeng net fish fifteen hundred students Chan
Senses.Note: Sansheng asks Xuefeng what a fish that has escaped the net eats. Xuefeng says he will answer when Sansheng is out of the net; Sansheng then delivers this rebuke. Feiyin, Poshan, Wanru, Sanyi, Sanshan, and Qianyan separately comment or write verses on the exchange. Their judgments divide between Sansheng's daring challenge and Xuefeng's deflection. The exact line is Sansheng's quoted speech, not the later commentators' own accusation.
